question: You see a patient with red, scaly plaques and wish to distinguish psoriasis from lichen planus at the bedside. Which single finding most reliably points AWAY from psoriasis and towards lichen planus?

answers.text: Pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign) after scraping the scale

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The Auspitz sign — pinpoint bleeding after graded scraping — is a feature OF psoriasis and supports that diagnosis, not lichen planus.

answers.text: Silvery-white scale that flakes off like candle wax

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The candle-grease sign (silvery scale flaking in layers) is characteristic of psoriasis, not lichen planus, and reflects the parakeratotic scale of accelerated keratinocyte turnover.

answers.text: Violaceous flat-topped papules with fine white Wickham striae and no Auspitz sign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lichen planus produces violaceous (purple), flat-topped, polygonal papules with fine white lacy Wickham striae and crucially does NOT show the Auspitz sign — this colour–surface–sign combination is the decisive discriminator from psoriasis.

answers.text: New lesions appearing along a scratch line (Koebner phenomenon)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The Koebner phenomenon occurs in both psoriasis and lichen planus (and in vitiligo), so it cannot be used to distinguish between them.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the contrast: psoriasis gives red plaques with silvery scale and a positive Auspitz sign in an extensor distribution; lichen planus gives violaceous flat-topped papules with Wickham striae and NO Auspitz sign in a flexural distribution.

Well done. The lichen planus–psoriasis contrast turns on violaceous versus erythematous colour, flat-topped papules versus raised plaques, Wickham striae versus silvery scale, and absent versus positive Auspitz sign.
